offered_action_specs.description: Roll one service back to the settings it ran before its latest deploy, as the deploy log records them. Code plans it from that log, not from your tools' results, so you can name it even when they cannot see deploys: if the log holds no deploy of that service to undo, or the service changed since, code refuses it. Its container is recreated, so the service pauses while it restarts. Money already booked wrong stays wrong: a rollback stops new damage, and repairs nothing.

proposed.why: The evidence points to the provider no longer answering: read timeouts opened payments-api's circuit breaker. Nothing on our side changed to cause it, so I am diagnosing now rather than spend the last call.

diagnosis.hypothesis:
From about 16:43:20 the payment provider (fake-provider, an outside company) stopped answering in time. payments-api's calls to /v1/payments and /v1/refunds began failing with ReadTimeout (result no_answer, about 1.5/s on payments), while successful 200 answers dropped toward zero.

The requests that waited out the timeout produce the 5.6 s p95. The repeated timeouts tripped the circuit breaker (PROVIDER_BREAKER=on). payments-api now refuses most calls without sending them and returns 503, leaving each payment pending. That gives the 97% 5xx.

No change on our side explains it: every container, the provider's included, was created together at 16:41:45, and traffic was healthy for over a minute after. The breaker is doing its job and is not the root cause.

Open questions: why the provider hangs (we see only its answers), and whether these payments later succeed at the provider, since a timed-out call may still have been processed. I did not run a money check.

evidence.shows: payments-api 503s rise from about 0.04/s to about 10.3/s from 16:43:31, while 201s fall to about 0.18/s. This confirms the alert's error symptom.
payments-api ERROR logs: 'provider unavailable; payment left pending', with '/v1/payments not sent: the circuit breaker is open'. The same payment ids recur, as clients retry.

From 16:43:21, provider attempts end in ReadTimeout (no_answer) on /v1/payments (about 1.4-1.6/s) and /v1/refunds (about 0.25/s). Provider 200s collapse at the same time. This is what opened the breaker.
Provider HTTP 500s stay low, about 0.1-0.24/s. Timeouts have no status code, so this metric hides them. The client metric shows only the answered calls falling to 0.
Answered provider calls stay fast (p95 about 5-8 ms). The latency is in calls that got no answer and waited out the read timeout, not in slow answers.
All services, the provider included, were created together at 16:41:45 with normal settings: a fresh start, not a targeted deploy. A rollback has no change to undo.

proposed_fix.target: fake-provider (external payment provider) / payments-api pending payments
proposed_fix.summary: Treat this as a provider outage. Escalate to the provider and check its status. Keep the circuit breaker on, so we do not pile load on it. Once the provider answers again and the breaker closes, check the payments and refunds left pending against the provider's records with a money check. Timed-out calls may have been processed by the provider, so confirm by webhook or provider record, not by blind re-charging. Do not roll back our services: none of them changed in a way that explains this.

diagnosis.blast_radius: This changes nothing on our side, so it adds no new risk. Until the provider recovers, payments and refunds keep failing fast with 503 and stay pending. The risk to manage is double-charging: retrying a payment whose timed-out call the provider actually processed. Idempotency keys and reconciliation must guard against that.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: Nothing to undo, since no change is made. If later evidence shows a fault on our side, for example a changed timeout or network setting in payments-api, revisit and roll back that service instead.
